{{Short description|none}}

The [[news media phone hacking scandal]] is a controversy over illegal acquisition of confidential information by news media organizations that reportedly occurred in the United Kingdom, the United States and Australia between 1995 and 2011. This article includes reference lists for various topics relating to that scandal.

==Overview and topics==
These lists are organized according to the topics shown below in blue type.

By 2002, the practice of [[Phone hacking scandal reference lists#Publications mentioned in the ICO report|publications using private investigators]] to acquire confidential information was widespread,<ref name=WhatPricePrivacy/> with some individuals using illegal methods.<ref name=GuardianRees20020921a>{{cite news|last=McLagan|first=Graeme|title=Fraudster squad- Graeme McLagan on the black economy run by corrupt police and private detectives|url=https://www.theguardian.com/uk/2002/sep/21/privacy2|accessdate=28 August 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=20 September 2002}}</ref><ref 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=21 September 2011}}</ref> [[Phone hacking scandal reference lists#Victims|Victims]] of these illegal methods included celebrities,<ref Individuals included on these lists are reportedly involved as victims, perpetrators, investigators, solicitors, or responsible oversight officials in the phone hacking scandal. Illegal acquisition of information was allegedly accomplished by accessing private voicemail accounts, hacking into computers, making false statements to officials to obtain confidential information, entrapment,<ref name=NYTimesMcMullan201111>{{cite news|last=Lyall|first=Sarah|title=British Inquiry Is Told Hacking Is Worthy Tool|newspaper=New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2011/11/30/world/europe/british-hacking-scandal-widens-to-government-secrets.html?pagewanted=all|date=29 Nov 2011|accessdate=4 Aug 2012}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Undercover at the News of the World|newspaper=BBC Channel 4|url=http://www.channel4.com/programmes/undercover-at-the-news-of-the-world/episode-guide/series-1/episode-1|date=2 Aug 2012|accessdate=4 Aug 2012}}</ref> blackmail,<ref name=GuardianFallon20120803>{{cite news|last=O'Carroll|first=Lisa|title=Kieren Fallon says he felt suicidal over News of the World sting|newspaper=The Guardian|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2012/aug/03/kieren-fallon-suicidal-news-of-the-world-sting|date=3 Aug 2012|accessdate=4 Aug 2012}}</ref> burglaries,<ref name=DaviesRees20110609>{{cite news|last=Davies|first=Nick|title=The NoW's merchant of secrets|url=http://www.nickdavies.net/2011/07/08/the-nows-merchant-of-secrets/|accessdate=19 September 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=9 June 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120327074724/http://www.nickdavies.net/2011/07/08/the-nows-merchant-of-secrets/|archive-date=27 March 2012|url-status=dead}}</ref> theft of mobile phones<ref>{{cite news|last=Somaiya|first=Ravi|title=Murdoch Inquiry Extends to Cellphone Theft|newspaper=New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2012/07/24/world/europe/murdoch-probe-extends-to-cellphone-theft.html?hp|date=23 July 2012|accessdate=23 July 2012}}</ref> and making payments to officials in exchange for confidential information. The kind of information acquired illegally may have include private communication, physical location of individuals, bank account records, medical records, phone bills, tax files, and organizational strategies.<ref name=DavisRees20110609>{{cite news|last=Davies|first=Nick|title=The NoW's merchant of secrets|url=http://www.nickdavies.net/2011/07/08/the-nows-merchant-of-secrets/|accessdate=18 September 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=9 June 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120327074724/http://www.nickdavies.net/2011/07/08/the-nows-merchant-of-secrets/|archive-date=27 March 2012|url-status=dead}}</ref>

There is evidence that illegal acquisition of confidential information continued at least into 2010.<ref name=GuardianMcDonagh201209>{{cite news|last=O'Carroll|first=Lisa|title=Labour MP Siobhain McDonagh sues News International and the Sun|url=https://www.theguardian.com/uk/2012/sep/10/siobhain-mcdonagh-labour-mp-news-international|date=10 Sep 2012|accessdate=10 Sep 2012}}</ref><ref name=GuardianAkers20120723>{{cite news|last=O'Carroll|first=Lisa|title=Leveson inquiry: NI staff 'appeared to have data from stolen phones'|newspaper=The Guardian|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2012/jul/23/leveson-inquiry-news-international-stolen-data|date=23 July 2012|accessdate=25 Sep 2012}}</ref> Solicitors representing victims were targeted for surveillance by news organizations being sued as recently as 2011.<ref name=GuardianLewis20111107/>

==Surveillance targets==
These are lists of individuals who were targeted for surveillance beyond simple phone hacking by news media organizations. Some were targeted simply to acquire information for developing a story but others were vocal critics of news media companies and may have been targeted to obtain information with which to influence criminal investigations, civil suits, and Parliamentary hearings.

===Critics of news media organizations===

This list includes a serving police officer, two solicitors with clients suing [[News International]], and a Member of Parliament. Dates in parentheses indicate the approximate date that surveillance was initiated.

# '''Cook, David'''; (June 2002) While investigating [[Jonathan Rees]] and Sid Fillery in connection with the 1987 murder of [[Daniel Morgan (private investigator)|Daniel Morgan]], Metropolitan Police detective chief superintendent Cook reportedly became a surveillance target of [[Glenn Mulcaire]], who was working for ''News of the World.''<ref name=GuardianRees20110608/><ref name=TelegraphHacking20110713>{{cite news|author1=Rainey, Sarah  |author2=Andrew Blenkinsop |name-list-style=amp |title=Phone hacking: who's who in the News International scandal|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/uknews/phone-hacking/8635999/Phone-hacking-whos-who-in-the-News-International-scandal.html|accessdate=15 August 2011|newspaper=The Telegraph|date=13 July 2011}}</ref><ref name=GuardianCook20110706>{{cite news|last=Davies|first=Nick|title=News of the World surveillance of detective: what Rebekah Brooks knew|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2011/jul/06/news-of-the-world-rebekah-brooks|accessdate=27 August 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=6 July 2011}}</ref> Fillery reportedly used his relationship with Alex Marunchak at ''News of the World'' to arrange for Mulcaire to obtain Cook's home address, his internal payroll number at the Metropolitan police, his date of birth and figures for the amount that he and his wife were paying for their mortgage. [[Metropolitan Police role in the News International phone hacking scandal#Operation Nigeria (1999)|Surveillance of Cook]] is also reported to have involved physically following him and his young children, attempts to access his voicemail and that of his wife, and possibly attempts to send a "Trojan horse" email in an attempt to steal information from his computer. Documents reportedly in the possession of the Scotland Yard shows that "Mulcaire did this on the instructions of [[Greg Miskiw]], the paper's assistant editor and a close friend of Marunchak." Attempts also appear to have been made to open letters which had been left in Cook's external postbox, indicating a "possible attempt to pervert the course of justice." [[Rebekah Brooks]], then editor for ''News of the World'', was aware of the surveillance.<ref name=GuardianBrooks20110706>{{cite news|last=Davies|first=Nick|title=News of the World surveillance of detective: what Rebekah Brooks knew|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2011/jul/06/news-of-the-world-rebekah-brooks|accessdate=18 September 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=6 July 2011}}</ref>
# '''[[Tom Watson, Baron Watson of Wyre Forest|Watson, Tom]]'''; (September 2009) Watson had been at odds with News International since 2006, when he quit as Government Minister and signed a letter demanding that [[Tony Blair]] resign as Prime Minister. [[Rebekah Brooks]], then editor of News International's ''[[The Sun (United Kingdom)|The Sun]]'', reportedly stated she would not forgive him for this and that she would pursue Watson for the rest of his life.<ref name=BirminghamPostWatson20110708>{{cite news|last=Walker|first=Jonathan|title=The Tom Watson Story: The man who took on Rupert Murdoch and won|newspaper=Birmingham Post- News Blog|url=http://blogs.birminghampost.net/news/2011/07/the-tom-watson-story-the-man-w.html|date=8 July 2011|accessdate=21 July 2012|archive-date=17 July 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110717004650/http://blogs.birminghampost.net/news/2011/07/the-tom-watson-story-the-man-w.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> Watson found himself targeted, with strangers going through his rubbish and harassing his family.<ref name=BirminghamPostWatson20110708/> As a member of the [[Culture, Media and Sport Select Committee]], he confronted News International executives with critical observations and probing questions. While the Committee was holding hearings leading to a formal report on phone hacking, three as yet unnamed News International executives arranged for Watson to be put under surveillance by private investigator and former policeman, [[Derek Webb]].<ref name=GuardianWatson2011>{{cite news|last=O'Carroll|first=Lisa|title=James Murdoch's lawyers confirm Tom Watson was put under surveillance|newspaper=The Guardian|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2011/dec/07/james-murdoch-tom-watson-surveillance|date=7 Dec 2011|accessdate=21 July 2012}}</ref>
# '''Lewis, Mark'''; (May 2010) While Lewis was representing claimants against ''[[News of the World]]'' for phone hacking, its parent company, [[News International]], hired Derek Webb to put Lewis and his family under surveillance. This was reportedly part of an attempt to gather evidence for false smears about his private life and thereby interfere with his ability to represent clients.<ref name=GuardianLewis20111107>{{cite news|last=Davies|first=Nick|title=News of the World hired investigators to spy on hacking victims' lawyers|newspaper=The Guardian|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2011/nov/07/news-world-investigator-spy-lawyers|date=7 Nov 2011|accessdate=21 July 2012}}</ref> The attempt to discredit the solicitors may also have been intended to protect the reputation of [[Andy Coulson]], formerly editor of ''[[News of the World]]'' who subsequently became head of communications for the Conservative Party and senior media adviser to Prime Minister [[David Cameron]].<ref name=TelegraphSurveillance20111107>{{cite news|last=Rayner|first=Gordon|title=News of the World hired private eye to spy on phone hacking victims' lawyers|newspaper=The Telegraph|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/uknews/phone-hacking/8875395/News-of-the-World-hired-private-eye-to-spy-on-phone-hacking-victims-lawyers.html|date=7 Nov 2011|accessdate=21 July 2012}}</ref> A dossier including video taken of his ex-wife and daughter was given to [[Tom Crone (barrister)|Tom Crone]], the senior legal manager at News International. [[James Murdoch]] was executive chairman of the company at the time.<ref name="GuardianLewis20111107"/><ref name=NYTimes20120415>{{cite news|last=Chozick|first=Amy|title=News Corporation's Pursuer Had Modest Start|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2012/04/16/business/media/mark-lewis-lawyer-in-phone-hacking-case-chases-news-corporation-in-us.html?pagewanted=all|newspaper=The New York Times|date=15 April 2012|accessdate=20 July 2012}}</ref><ref name=GuardianPike20120522/><ref name=TelegraphLewis20111130>{{cite news|title=Leveson Inquiry: 'News International tried to destroy my life,' hacking lawyer claims|newspaper=The Telegraph|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/uknews/leveson-inquiry/8926467/Leveson-Inquiry-News-International-tried-to-destroy-my-life-hacking-lawyer-claims.html|date=30 November 2011|accessdate=21 July 2012}}</ref> Lewis told the Leveson Inquiry that "News International sought to destroy my life, and very nearly succeeded."<ref name="TelegraphLewis20111130" />
# '''Harris, Charlotte'''; (January 2011) Like Mark Lewis, Harris also came under surveillance by an agent of [[News International]] while representing clients suing the company in relation to phone hacking by ''[[News of the World]]''." Her pursuit of evidence for her clients led to disclosure of information that reportedly resulted in the firing of [[Ian Edmondson]] from ''News of the World'' and the resignation of the prime minister's media adviser, [[Andy Coulson]]. Also like Lewis, both she and her family were followed and video-taped, with a dossier given to News International's [[Tom Crone (barrister)|Tom Crone]]. The private investigator, Derek Webb, was asked to establish that Harris was having an affair with someone it turned out that she had never met. Over the years, News International had engaged Webb to target more than 90 people.<ref name=GuardianLewis20111107/><ref name=GuardianWatson2011/><ref name=TelegraphSurveillance20111107/><ref name=NYTimes20120415/>

===Other surveillance targets===

In November 2011, Channel 4 News disclosed a list of 153 people upon whom private investigator [[Derek Webb]] was reportedly asked by the ''[[News of the World]]'' to carry out surveillance between 2003 and 2011. ==Solicitors==
This is an alphabetical list of solicitors involved in the phone hacking scandal.

===Alleged victims of phone hacking===
The list of alleged victims of phone hacking includes some solicitors. [[The Law Society]] noted that it would be a serious offence if this hacking was done with the intention of affecting judicial outcomes.<ref name=Channel14Stephens20110722>{{cite news|title=Solicitors' phones 'hacked by News of the World'|url=http://www.channel4.com/news/solicitors-phones-hacked-by-news-of-the-world|accessdate=29 August 2011|publisher=Channel 4 News|date=22 July 2011}}</ref>

# '''[[Kirsty Brimelow]]'''; prominent criminal barrister who has represented clients in rape and murder trials.<ref name=GuardianClaims20120907>{{cite news|author1=O'Carroll, Lisa  |author2=Josh Halliday |name-list-style=amp |title=News International may face 230 new claims over alleged phone hacking|newspaper=The Guardian|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2012/sep/07/news-international-230-phone-hacking-claims|date=7 Sep 2012|accessdate=9 Sep 2012}}</ref>
# '''Harris, Charlotte'''; solicitor representing alleged victims of phone hacking<ref name=GuardianLewis20111107/><ref name=GuardianWatson2011/><ref name=TelegraphSurveillance20111107/><ref name=Channel14Stephens20110722/>
# '''Lewis, Mark'''; solicitor representing as many as 70 alleged victims of phone hacking including Milly Dowler's family<ref name=Channel14Stephens20110722/>
# '''[[Mark Stephens (solicitor)|Stephens, Mark]]'''; solicitor whose clients have included James Hewitt, who allegedly had an affair with Princess Diana, and WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange.<ref name=Channel14Stephens20110722/>
# '''Winskell, Robin'''; sports attorney who has represented prominent footballers in disciplinary trials, FIFA arbritrations, and libel cases.<ref name=GuardianClaims20120907/>

===Representing victims of illegal acquisition of confidential information===
# '''Tamsin Allen''';
# '''Charlotte Harris'''; Partner at the London law firm [[Mishcon de Reya]]<ref>{{cite news|title=Charlotte Harris: Nowhere to hide, says the lawyer on Murdoch~'s case|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/people/profiles/charlotte-harris-nowhere-to-hide-says-the-lawyer-on-murdochs-case-2269242.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220618/https://www.independent.co.uk/news/people/profiles/charlotte-harris-nowhere-to-hide-says-the-lawyer-on-murdochs-case-2269242.html |archive-date=18 June 2022 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live|accessdate=26 September 2011|newspaper=The Independent|date=18 April 2010}}</ref> who represented Max Clifford, who received £400,000 from ''[[News of the World]]''.<ref name=NYTimesRoyals20100901/><ref name=GuardianClifford20100309>{{cite news|author1=Davies, Nick  |author2=Rob Evans |name-list-style=amp |title=Max Clifford drops News of the World phone hacking action in £1m deal|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2010/mar/09/clifford-news-of-the-world-phone-hacking|accessdate=20 August 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=9 March 2010}}</ref> misrepresented as advanced payment for stories. They also paid Harris's costs. Harris has gone on to act for numerous individuals with hacking claims.
#'''Steven Heffer''', Partner and Head of Media & Privacy at London law firm Collyer Bristow LLP, who acted for about 80 victims.
# '''Mark Lewis'''; As solicitor for the Professional Footballers' Association in 2005, Lewis realized that ''[[News of the World]]'' was using phone hacking as the basis for a story concerning [[Gordon Taylor (footballer)|Gordon Taylor]]. In 2008, Lewis became the first solicitor to bring a claim for a client relating to phone hacking and went on to win a settlement from the newspaper for phone hacking. Taylor received £700,000.<ref>{{cite news|last=Bowcott|first=Owen|title='No-win, no-fee' brought down News of the World, says hacking victims' lawyer|url=https://www.theguardian.com/law/2011/jul/19/no-win-no-fee-phone-hacking|accessdate=25 September 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=19 July 2011}}</ref> While represent clients against News International, the company hired a private investigator to put Lewis and his family under surveillance.<ref name=GuardianPike20120522>{{cite news|last=O'Carroll|first=Lisa|title=Surveillance of phone-hacking victims' solicitors was justified, says lawyer|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2012/may/22/surveillance-phone-hacking-lawyers|newspaper=The Guardian|date=22 May 2012|accessdate=20 July 2012}}</ref> Lewis lost his position at George Davies Solicitors L.L.P because the firm did not want to be involved in his suits.<ref name=NYTimes20120415/> In 2011 Lewis acted for the family of Milly Dowler achieving a record £3 million deal. He joined Taylor Hampton Solicitors in London. Lewis has represented about 100 claimants against the News of the World and other newspapers and has explored filing phone hacking suits in the US.<ref name="NYTimes20120415"/>
# '''Gerald Shamash''';
# '''David Sherborne''';<ref name=GuardianEmail20120718>{{cite news|last=O'Carroll|first=Lisa|title=Phone hacking: 'significant' email from News International executive emerges|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2012/jul/18/phone-hacking-email-news-international|newspaper=The Guardian|date=18 July 2012|accessdate=20 July 2012}}</ref>
# [[Mark Stephens (solicitor)|Mark Stephens]]; partner at the London law firm Finers Stephens Innocent representing 11 tranche 1 claimants, all of which settled pre-trial. He is reportedly representing a dozen claimants in tranche 2.
# '''Mark Thomson'''; among others, represented [[Siobhain McDonagh]] MP in relation to invasion of privacy allegedly associated with attempts by agents of ''[[The Sun (UK)|The Sun]]'' to break codes necessary to access information on her stolen mobile phone.<ref name=GuardianMcDonagh201209/>
# [[Hugh Tomlinson]]; QC<ref name=GuardianEmail20120718/> Barrister, advised the high court around September 2012 that 395 people had applied for disclosure of phone-hacking evidence from the Met, that 124 phone-hacking claims had been accepted by the [[News International]] compensation fund, and that something under 300 new claims would be forthcoming.<ref name=GuardianClaims20120907/>
# Chris Waters, Head of Dispute Resolution at London Law Firm Malletts represents Former Boxing World Champion [[Chris Eubank]] and ex-wife Karron Stephen-Martin in News International Hacking Claims. Waters also acts for numerous other victims in claims against News International.

In 2011 a group was formed for the Claimant's solicitors. In addition to Harris and Lewis, several solicitors brought claims including Tamsin Allen, Mark Thomson and Gerald Shamash. Allen was the Claimant Group's first co-ordinator, Thomson took over after Allen settled her claims. There were several other solicitors involved in the group, including [[Mark Stephens (solicitor)|Mark Stephens]].

===Otherwise involved in phone hacking scandal===
# '''Lawrence Abramson'''; As solicitor at [[Harbottle & Lewis]], Abramson sent a letter 29 May 2007 stating H&L's review of emails provided by [[News International]] did not indicate involvement in phone hacking by other than Clive Goodman.<ref name=BBCEmails20110710>{{cite news|last=Peston|first=Robert|title=News International found 'smoking gun' e-mails in 2007|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/business-14099102|accessdate=18 August 2011|newspaper=BBC News- Business|date=10 July 2011}}</ref> This letter was subsequently used by News International executives to maintain that Goodman was a single "rogue reporter."<ref name="smoking gun">{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/business-14099102|title=News International found 'smoking gun' e-mails in 2007|work=BBC News |date=2011-07-12 |accessdate=2011-07-17}}</ref> When '''[[Ken Macdonald|Lord Kenneth Macdonald]]''' reviewed the emails again in July 2011, he reported "evidence of serious criminal offences" including payments to police.<ref name=BBCProbe>{{cite news|title=Phone hacking: Scotland Yard boosts probe team|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-14222771|accessdate=20 August 2011|newspaper=BBC News|date=21 July 2011}}</ref>
# '''Pike, Julian'''; Partner at Farrer & Co; represented the [[News Group Newspapers]] subsidiary of [[News International]] during the 2008 settlement negotiations leading to payment of £425,000 plus costs to '''[[Gordon Taylor (footballer)|Gordon Taylor]]'''. Pike told the Culture, Media and Sport Committee on 19 October 2011 that he had informed News International of evidence suggesting "a powerful case" could be made that three ''[[News of the World]]'' journalists had illegally accessed confidential information. News International maintained through 2009 that only '''[[Clive Goodman]]''' had been involved. Pike also told the Committee that '''Colin Myler''' met with James Murdoch on 27 May 2008, after Pike had received a copy of the new evidence which had been emailed by '''Tom Crone''' to Myler. This meeting was in addition to Myler's meeting with Murdoch and Crone 10 June 2008. Pike had not reported earlier that senior News International personnel had misled Parliament because of professional obligations to his client. Farrer & Co. also represents Queen Elizabeth II.<ref>{{cite news|last=Robinson|first=James|title=Phone hacking: NI lawyer says he knew its 'rogue reporter' defence was wrong|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2011/oct/19/phone-hacking-lawyer-ni-rogue-reporter|accessdate=19 October 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=19 October 2011}}</ref> In 2011, Pike advised News International that [[News International phone hacking scandal reference lists#Surveillance targets|Mark Lewis and Charlotte Harris should be put under surveillance]] while they were representing clients suing the company.<ref name=NYTimes20120415/> As a result, both of them and their families were followed and video-taped. Pike continued to characterize this apparent attempt to find information with which to discredit opposing solicitors as "unusual" but "justified" and "would do it again tomorrow," even after News International acknowledged that it was "deeply inappropriate."<ref name=GuardianPike20120522/> Farrer & Co. also wrote to Lewis threatening to enjoin him from accepting more clients that wanted to sue ''News of the World'' over phone hacking.<ref name=TelegraphSurveillance20111107/> Pike also discussed the possibility with News International's legal affairs manager, [[Tom Crone (barrister)|Tom Crone]], of making charges of professional misconduct against Lewis and Harris.<ref name=GuardianWatson2011/> Lewis told the [[Leveson Inquiry]] that "News International sought to destroy my life, and very nearly succeeded."<ref name=TelegraphLewis20111130/>

==Publications mentioned in the ICO report==
This is a list of newspapers and magazines listed in the [[Information Commissioner's Office]] (ICO) report of May 2006 titled ''What Price Privacy?''. The publications are listed in order of the number of pieces of data each paid a private investigator for.

This report presented what had been learned from the ICO investigation named [[Operation Motorman (ICO investigation)|Operation Motorman]], which was begun in 2002.<ref name=WhatPricePrivacy>{{cite web|title=What Price Privacy?|url=http://www.ico.gov.uk/~/media/documents/library/Corporate/Research_and_reports/WHAT_PRICE_PRIVACY.ashx|publisher=Information Commissioner's Office|date=10 May 2006|accessdate=2011-08-20|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110829133733/http://www.ico.gov.uk/~/media/documents/library/Corporate/Research_and_reports/WHAT_PRICE_PRIVACY.ashx|archive-date=29 August 2011}}</ref> "Information Commissioner [[Richard Thomas (solicitor)|Richard Thomas]] ... revealed that hundreds of journalists may have illegally bought private information and named a list of newspapers and magazines using one particular information agency... Numerous invoices [were found] addressed to newspapers and magazines which detailed prices for providing the journalists with personal information ... Here is the table listing the [name of the publication] followed by number of pieces of data paid for and the number of journalists involved."<ref name=Pressgazette20021215>{{cite news |url=http://www.pressgazette.co.uk/story.asp?storycode=36439 |title=Info chief's broadside at press over data crimes |work=Press Gazette |date=15 December 2002 |accessdate=14 August 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120111213136/http://www.pressgazette.co.uk/story.asp?storycode=36439 |archive-date=11 January 2012 }}</ref>

==Individuals acknowledging that confidential information was acquired illegally==
[[File:Sean Hoare.jpg|thumb|[[Sean Hoare]] claimed he was encouraged by [[Andy Coulson]], editor of ''[[News of the World]]'' to hack phones.<ref name=NYTimesGoodman20100905>{{cite news|last=Van Natta Jr, Don, Jo Becker, and Grahm Bowley|title=Tabloid Hack Attack on Royals, and Beyond|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2010/09/05/magazine/05hacking-t.html?pagewanted=1|accessdate=17 August 2011|newspaper=New York Times|date=1 September 2010}}</ref>]]

This is a chronological list of individuals that acknowledged acquiring confidential information illegally themselves or, from first-hand experience, alleged the practice was widespread by news media companies. Dates in parentheses indicates approximately when each individual made the admission.

As of 15 December 2010, ''[[The Guardian]]'' reported that more than 20 journalists who worked for ''[[News of the World]]'' had told ''The Guardian'', ''[[The New York Times]]'' or [[Dispatches (TV programme)|Channel 4's ''Dispatches'']] that "illegal activity assisted by private investigators was commonplace and well known to executives, including [[Andy Coulson]]."<ref name=GuardianMiller20101215>{{cite news|last=Davies|first=Nick|title=Phone Hacking sienna Miller Evidence|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2010/dec/15/phone-hacking-sienna-miller-evidence|accessdate=11 October 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=15 December 2010}}</ref> Coulson has denied having knowledge of phone hacking while he was editor at ''[[News of the World]]''.

# [[Clive Goodman]]; (2007) royal correspondent for ''[[News of the World]]''<ref name=GuardianGoodman20061120/>
# [[Glenn Mulcaire]]; (2007) private investigator<ref name=GuardianGoodman20061120/>

# [[Piers Morgan]]; (2007) former editor of the ''[[Daily Mirror]]'', former editor of the ''[[News of the World]]'', and former show business editor of the ''[[The Sun (United Kingdom)|Sun]]'' stated that "loads of newspaper journalists were doing it. Clive Goodman, the ''[[News of the World]]'' reporter, has been made the [[scapegoat]] for a widespread practice."<ref name=IndependentWidespread20110718>{{cite news|author1=Moore, James  |author2=Ian Burrell |name-list-style=amp |title=Hacking was endemic at the 'Mirror', says former reporter|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/media/press/hacking-was-endemic-at-the-mirror-says-former-reporter-2319039.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220618/https://www.independent.co.uk/news/media/press/hacking-was-endemic-at-the-mirror-says-former-reporter-2319039.html |archive-date=18 June 2022 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live|accessdate=23 August 2011|newspaper=The Independent|date=18 July 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Robinson|first=James|title=Piers Morgan under pressure to return to UK from America|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2011/aug/04/piers-morgan-under-pressure-phone-hacking|accessdate=25 August 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=4 August 2011}}</ref>

==Individuals who worked for both News International and the police==
[[File:News Internaltional Building in London.JPG|thumb|upright|By mid-2012 formal charges had been filed against many News International journalists and executives, including former chief executive [[Rebekah Brooks]].]]

This is an alphabetical list of individuals who at various times worked for both [[News International]] and the [[Metropolitan Police Service]].

# [[Andy Hayman]] was with the [[Essex Police]] from 1978 until 1998, when he transferred to the [[Metropolitan Police Service]]. He became [[Chief Constable]] for the [[Norfolk Constabulary]] in 2002 but returned to the Met in February 2005.<ref>{{cite news|last=Cowan|first=Rosie|title=The threat is real. London is an iconic site for another attack|url=https://www.theguardian.com/uk/2005/sep/29/terrorism.july71|accessdate=16 October 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=29 September 2005}}</ref> Hayman was in charge of the Royal Household/Goodman Inquiry in 2006. He resigned from the Met in December 2007 during an investigation of reportedly lavish entertainment expenditures for "long lunches and dinners with ''[[News of the World]]'' journalists at a time when the newspaper was under investigation for phone hacking."<ref name=TelegraphHayman20110724>{{cite news|last=Mendick|first=Robert|title=Phone hacking: Police chief Andy Hayman paid for champagne dinners with News of the World journalists|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/uknews/phone-hacking/8656580/Phone-hacking-Police-chief-Andy-Hayman-paid-for-champagne-dinners-with-News-of-the-World-journalists.html|accessdate=16 October 2011|newspaper=The Telegraph|date=24 July 2011}}</ref> Two months later he was hired by [[News International]], where he wrote an article for ''[[The Times]]'' defending the police investigation he led, maintaining that there were "perhaps a handful" of hacking victims.<ref name=NYTimesRoyals20100901/><ref name=TelegraphHayman20110724/>
# [[Alex Marunchak]] worked as a freelance Ukrainian language interpreter for the [[Metropolitan Police Service]] between 1980 and 2000 while he was also an executive for ''[[News of the World]]'', where he worked from 1981 to 2006. He provide "interpretation and translation services for victims, witnesses and suspects of crime who do not speak English."<ref>{{cite news|last=Hughes|first=Mark|title=Phone Hacking: News of the World executive 'worked as police translator'|newspaper=The Telegraph|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/uknews/phone-hacking/8646307/Phone-Hacking-News-of-the-World-executive-worked-as-police-translator.html|date=19 July 2011|accessdate=10 August 2012}}</ref> Marunchak was a regular customer of private investigator [[Jonathan Rees]], who was reportedly purchasing information from improper sources. No evidence became public that Marunchak or other journalists had committed criminal offences or that they were aware of how Rees acquired the information.<ref name="GuardianRees20020921b" /> Marunchak reportedly arranged for [[Glenn Mulcaire]], then doing work for ''News of the World'', to [[Metropolitan Police role in the News International phone hacking scandal#Operation Nigeria (1999)|conduct surveillance on the detective]] investigating Rees and his partner, Sid Fillery, for murder.<ref name="GuardianBrooks20110706"/>
# [[John Stevens, Baron Stevens of Kirkwhelpington]] was Met commissioner from 2000 to 2005. He has been credited with reopening communication between the news media and the police after his predecessor, [[Sir Paul Condon]] had all but closed it down in the mid-1990s with his anti-corruption drive at Scotland Yard.<ref name=GuardianInquiries20110901>{{cite news|last=Laville|first=Sandra|title=Police contact with media to be evaluated by two inquiries|url=https://www.theguardian.com/uk/2011/sep/01/police-contact-media-inquiries-evaluated|accessdate=7 September 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=1 September 2011}}</ref> After retiring, he wrote a column for the ''[[News of the World]]''. In his autobiography, he stated that he had "worked hard to foster good relations with newspapers and had made himself 'available' to editors including [[Rebekah Brooks]] (then Wade) at ''[[The Sun (United Kingdom)|The Sun]]'' and [[Andy Coulson]], then at the ''[[News of the World]]''." His diary, which may record meetings between him and [[News International]] executives between February 2000 to January 2005, went missing but was found in October 2011 at New Scotland Yard.<ref>{{cite news|title=Scotland Yard finds former chief's Lord Stevens' diary|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-15260810|accessdate=16 October 2011|newspaper=BBC News|date=11 October 2011}}</ref> In March 2011, he was chairman of security firm Axiom International.{{citation needed|date=June 2020}}
# [[Neil Wallis]] worked for [[News International]] from 1987 to 1998 and again from 2003 to 2009. He then started his own public relations firm, Chamy Media, which provided "strategic communication advice and support" to the Met on a part-time basis from October 2009 to September 2010.<ref>{{cite news|title=Met Chief Under Pressure Over NOTW Consultant|url=http://news.sky.com/home/uk-news/article/16030210|accessdate=16 October 2011|newspaper=Sky News|date=15 July 2011}}</ref> Wallis's firm was paid £24,000 by the Met at the same time Wallis received more than £25,000 from [[News International]] for providing "crime exclusives" using details of Met investigations.<ref name=TelegraphWallis201109>{{cite news|author1=Winnett, Robert  |author2=Mark Hughes |name-list-style=amp |title=Phone hacking: News International paid Neil Wallis while he was at Scotland Yard|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/uknews/phone-hacking/8785470/Phone-hacking-News-International-paid-Neil-Wallis-while-he-was-at-Scotland-Yard.html|accessdate=23 September 2011|newspaper=The Telegraph|date=23 September 2011}}</ref><ref name=TelegraphStephenson20110901>{{cite news|title=Phone hacking: Sir Paul Stephenson faces questions of health spa stay|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/uknews/phone-hacking/8642818/Phone-hacking-Sir-Paul-Stephenson-faces-questions-of-health-spa-stay.html|accessdate=1 September 2011|newspaper=The Telegraph|date=16 July 2011}}</ref> Wallis was arrested in July 2011 on suspicion of conspiring to intercept communications<ref name=TelegraphWallis20110714>{{cite news|last=Orr|first=James|title=Former News of the World executive editor Neil Wallis ==Attempted suicides==
On 6 March 2012, Reuters reported that two senior journalists working for ''[[The Sun (United Kingdom)|The Sun]]'', a newspaper owned by [[News International]], appeared to have attempted suicide in the face of ongoing investigations relating to the phone hacking scandal. At that time, eleven current and former staff members of ''The Sun'' had been arrested on suspicion of bribing police or civil servants for information.<ref>{{cite news|last= Prodhan|first=Georgina|title=Two UK Murdoch journalists in apparent suicide bids|newspaper=Reuters|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-newscorp-journalists-pressure-idUSTRE8251HX20120306|date=6 March 2012|accessdate=20 May 2012}}</ref>

[[File:Final NOTW cover.jpeg|thumb| Public outrage over hacking [[Milly Dowler]]'s voice mail resulted in loss of advertising to ''[[News of the World]]'', leading to its being shut down after 168 years.<ref>{{cite news|last=Smith-Spark|first=Laura|title=Firms reconsider ad deals over newspaper phone hacking scandal|url=http://edition.cnn.com/2011/BUSINESS/07/06/uk.phonehacking.ads/index.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110708015005/http://edition.cnn.com/2011/BUSINESS/07/06/uk.phonehacking.ads/index.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=8 July 2011|accessdate=11 September 2011|newspaper=CNN|date=7 July 2011}}</ref><ref name=GuardianDowler20120509>{{cite news|last=Leigh|first=David|title=Milly Dowler: truth about deletion of messages may never be known|newspaper=The Guardian|url=https://www.theguardian.com/uk/2012/may/09/milly-dowler-deletion-messages|date=9 May 2012|accessdate=9 May 2012}}</ref>]]
